summary:
Greenland stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. It is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law, while criminal law and official document rules remain Danish.

Same-sex relations are lawful, and the territory's record on partnership and marriage has been permissive for three decades. Partnership law was adopted from the Danish model in 1996 and passed with virtually no debate, and it has since been replaced by the marriage law.

Same-sex marriage came into effect on 1 April 2016. Greenland adopted Danish legislation that had passed unanimously twice in Denmark, the first bill lapsing after Danish elections, and the local parliament enacted it without recorded opposition; it replaced the 1996 partnership law. The bishop of the established church supported it. Registered partnerships, in force from 1 July 1996, ceased to apply when the marriage law took effect.

Transgender Greenlanders may change the sex designation on official identity documents. A law passed by decree in 2016 allows legal sex change on the basis of self-determination, with no requirement for surgery, hormone therapy, sterilisation or medical diagnosis. Applicants must be over 18, state that they want their documentation changed, and observe a six-month reflection period before the request is confirmed. Greenlandic passports are available with an "X" sex descriptor alongside male and female.

Since 2010 the Criminal Code's Article 100 has prohibited hate speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other protected categories, and hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation carry penalty enhancements.

A Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination, passed in May 2024 and in force from 1 July 2024, prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics. It establishes an Equal Treatment Board to handle discrimination complaints and an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination. The state-funded Human Rights Council of Greenland works with the Danish Institute for Human Rights on human rights protection.

Public visibility is established but modest. The first pride parade was held in Nuuk on 15 May 2010 with about 1,000 attendees, and a Pride march has run annually since 2010. Gay life is described as low-key, integrated and non-violent. There is virtually no gay scene owing to the small, scattered population, though some Nuuk nightclubs and bars draw a mixed gay and straight crowd.

The national association LGBT Qaamaneq was founded in August 2014 to work for the political, cultural and social equality of lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, and is open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters.
tangentialFactors:
Greenland's legal position on gender identity and sexual orientation tracks Danish national frameworks, so shifts in Copenhagen's criminal or document law can travel to Nuuk without local legislative action; the 2016 marriage and sex-change measures were adopted from Danish instruments rather than drafted locally.

The territory's small, scattered population concentrates social and nightlife visibility in Nuuk, which shapes where a visitor is likely to encounter either an openly mixed environment or none at all.

Protection machinery is thin in staffing terms: an Equal Treatment Board and an Equality Council created in 2024 sit alongside a state-funded Human Rights Council that cooperates with the Danish Institute for Human Rights, so complaint handling and advocacy are split across bodies with different mandates.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state whether Greenland's hate-speech provision and hate-crime penalty enhancements have been applied in cases with a gender-identity dimension rather than sexual orientation; enforcement frequency is unresolved here.

Whether the Equal Treatment Board has issued decisions concerning gender identity or gender expression since 1 July 2024 is not sourced in this inventory.

Access to gender-affirming medical care in Greenland, as distinct from legal document change, is not covered by the sources and remains unresolved.

Entry, visa and border-screening practice for transgender travellers arriving in Greenland under Danish rules is not addressed in the inventory.
